title: Alcohol and Medications: Which Drugs Interact and Why
excerpt: Which medicines are risky with alcohol and why. The four interaction mechanisms, a drug-class table with links to every guide, how long to wait, and warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: Which medications interact with alcohol? How the four main mechanisms work, a class-by-class risk table, timing rules, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol interacts with a long list of common medicines, but the interactions fall into a handful of predictable patterns. Most of the serious ones come from four mechanisms: alcohol stacking on top of a drug that also slows your brain and breathing, alcohol and a drug both hitting the same organ (usually the liver or stomach), alcohol changing how fast your liver clears a drug, and a few drugs that block alcohol breakdown and make you violently sick. If you know which bucket your medicine falls into, you know roughly how careful you need to be. This hub explains each mechanism, gives a class-by-class table, and links to our detailed guide for each specific drug.

**The quick rules:** If your medicine makes you drowsy, treat alcohol as a serious risk, not a minor one. Read the Drug Facts or pharmacy label, because many prescriptions carry a printed alcohol warning for a reason. Never mix alcohol with opioids, benzodiazepines, or prescription sleeping pills. Don't drink while taking metronidazole or tinidazole. And if you're unsure, a pharmacist can check your exact medicine in a couple of minutes, for free, without an appointment.

> **This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist.** This article explains general mechanisms and label guidance. It can't account for your dose, your other medicines, your health conditions, or your drinking pattern, and those details change the answer. Don't stop or skip a prescribed medicine so you can drink without checking with your prescriber first, because stopping some drugs suddenly is dangerous in its own right. **Call 911 or get emergency help right away if** someone who mixed alcohol with a medicine is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue or gray lips, is having a seizure, has chest pain, or is confused in a way that isn't normal drunkenness. In the US, Poison Control is available 24/7 at **1-800-222-1222**.

## How Alcohol Interacts With Medications: The Four Main Mechanisms

Doctors split drug interactions into two broad types. A *pharmacokinetic* interaction means one substance changes how much of the other is in your blood (by changing how it's absorbed or broken down). A *pharmacodynamic* interaction means the two act on the same body system and their effects add up, even if blood levels don't change. Alcohol does both. In practice, almost every alcohol-medication interaction you'll read about fits one of these four patterns.

### 1. Stacking sedation (the most dangerous pattern)

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It slows brain activity, reaction time, and, at high enough levels, breathing. Many medicines do the same thing through overlapping pathways, especially by boosting the brain's main calming chemical, GABA. When you combine them, the effects add up and can more than add up.

At the mild end, that means you get drunker faster than you expect, feel foggy, and have worse coordination and judgment. At the dangerous end, it means slowed or stopped breathing, which is how most fatal alcohol-medication combinations kill people. The FDA added its strongest boxed warning to opioid and benzodiazepine labels in 2016 about combining those two drug classes, and alcohol acts on the same systems. This is the interaction category where "I only had a couple of drinks" is not reassuring.

Medicines in this group include opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines, prescription sleeping pills, gabapentin and pregabalin, muscle relaxants, sedating antihistamines, some antidepressants and antipsychotics, and certain seizure medicines.

### 2. Shared organ damage (liver, stomach, and blood sugar)

Some drugs aren't sedating, but they stress the same organ alcohol does.

- **Liver.** Acetaminophen is the classic example. A small part of each dose becomes a toxic by-product, and regular heavy drinking both speeds that up and drains the liver's antioxidant defenses. Other drugs with liver-toxicity warnings, such as the tuberculosis drug isoniazid, some antifungals, and isotretinoin (Accutane), add to the same concern.
- **Stomach.** Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate and erode the stomach lining. Alcohol does too. The US Drug Facts label for these painkillers carries a stomach-bleeding warning for people who have 3 or more drinks every day.
- **Blood sugar.** Alcohol blocks the liver from releasing stored glucose. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea (such as glipizide or glyburide), that can push your blood sugar dangerously low, sometimes hours later while you sleep.

### 3. Changing how fast your liver clears a drug

Your liver uses a family of enzymes (called cytochrome P450) to break down both alcohol and many medicines. Alcohol affects these enzymes in two opposite ways, depending on your drinking pattern:

- **Acute drinking** (a night out) can compete with some drugs for the same enzymes, so the drug may build up to higher levels than intended.
- **Chronic heavy drinking** can rev up some of these enzymes, so certain drugs get cleared faster and work less well, or get turned into toxic by-products faster.

Blood thinners like warfarin are the textbook case. A binge can push warfarin's effect up and raise bleeding risk, while steady heavy drinking can push it down. Either way your blood tests become harder to keep in range.

A related, rarer problem is "dose dumping." Some extended-release capsules are designed to release medicine slowly over many hours. Alcohol can dissolve certain coatings and release the dose all at once. An extended-release hydromorphone product was pulled from the US market in 2005 for exactly this reason. Many long-acting opioid labels now warn about it.

### 4. Drugs that block alcohol breakdown (the "Antabuse-like" reaction)

Normally your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, and then quickly clears the acetaldehyde. Disulfiram (Antabuse), a drug used on purpose to deter drinking, blocks that second step. Acetaldehyde builds up and causes flushing, pounding heart, nausea, vomiting, headache, and a drop in blood pressure.

A few other medicines carry label warnings for a similar reaction, most notably the antibiotics **metronidazole** (Flagyl) and **tinidazole**, and some older cephalosporin antibiotics. How often metronidazole actually causes the reaction is debated in the research, but the label says to avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 days after, and that's the advice to follow. Our guide on [metronidazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) covers the timing in detail, and if it's already happened, see [what to do if you accidentally drank on metronidazole](/never-hungover/accidentally-drank-on-metronidazole).

## Alcohol and Medication Interactions by Drug Class

Here's the hub table. Each row gives the main mechanism and a general risk level for a social drinker, plus a link to the full guide where we have one. "Risk" here means typical risk at normal doses; your situation may differ.

| Drug class | Common examples | Main mechanism | General risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opioid painkillers | [Oxycodone](/never-hungover/oxycodone-and-alcohol), hydrocodone, codeine, tramadol | Stacked sedation, slowed breathing | Avoid alcohol entirely |
| Benzodiazepines | [Xanax](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol), [Klonopin](/never-hungover/klonopin-and-alcohol), Valium, Ativan | Stacked sedation, slowed breathing | Avoid alcohol entirely |
| Prescription sleep drugs | Zolpidem (Ambien), eszopiclone, [trazodone](/never-hungover/trazodone-and-alcohol) ([all sleep aids](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol)) | Stacked sedation, complex sleep behaviors | Avoid alcohol entirely |
| Nerve pain and seizure drugs | [Gabapentin](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol), pregabalin, [Keppra](/never-hungover/keppra-and-alcohol) | Stacked sedation, dizziness | High; ask your prescriber |
| Muscle relaxants | [Cyclobenzaprine](/never-hungover/cyclobenzaprine-and-alcohol), methocarbamol ([all muscle relaxers](/never-hungover/muscle-relaxers-and-alcohol)) | Stacked sedation | High; avoid |
| Antibiotics (most) | [Amoxicillin](/never-hungover/amoxicillin-and-alcohol), [azithromycin](/never-hungover/azithromycin-and-alcohol), [doxycycline](/never-hungover/doxycycline-and-alcohol) | Usually no direct interaction; alcohol may slow recovery | Low to moderate |
| Antibiotics (reaction risk) | [Metronidazole](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol), tinidazole | Blocks acetaldehyde clearance | Avoid during and 3 days after |
| Acetaminophen | [Tylenol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol), many cold and flu combos | Liver toxicity | Moderate; count every source |
| NSAID painkillers | [Ibuprofen](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol), [Aleve](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol), [aspirin](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) | Stomach bleeding, kidney strain | Moderate; take with food |
| Blood thinners | Warfarin, [Eliquis](/never-hungover/eliquis-and-alcohol) ([overview](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol)) | Bleeding risk, warfarin level swings | Moderate to high; ask your prescriber |
| SSRIs and SNRIs | [Zoloft](/never-hungover/zoloft-and-alcohol), [Lexapro](/never-hungover/lexapro-and-alcohol), [Prozac](/never-hungover/prozac-and-alcohol), [Cymbalta](/never-hungover/cymbalta-and-alcohol) | Added drowsiness, worse mood; Cymbalta adds liver concern | Moderate |
| Other antidepressants | [Wellbutrin](/never-hungover/wellbutrin-and-alcohol), MAOIs | Seizure threshold (bupropion); blood pressure spikes with tyramine (MAOIs) | Moderate to high |
| Antipsychotics and mood stabilizers | [Seroquel](/never-hungover/seroquel-and-alcohol), [lithium](/never-hungover/lithium-and-alcohol) | Sedation; dehydration and lithium levels | High; ask your prescriber |
| ADHD stimulants | [Adderall](/never-hungover/adderall-and-alcohol), [Vyvanse](/never-hungover/vyvanse-and-alcohol), [Ritalin](/never-hungover/ritalin-and-alcohol) | Masks how drunk you are; heart strain | Moderate to high |
| Diabetes drugs | [Metformin](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol), insulin, sulfonylureas, [Mounjaro](/never-hungover/mounjaro-and-alcohol) | Low blood sugar; lactic acidosis warning (metformin) | Moderate; never drink on an empty stomach |
| Blood pressure and heart drugs | [Lisinopril](/never-hungover/lisinopril-and-alcohol), [amlodipine](/never-hungover/amlodipine-and-alcohol), [beta blockers](/never-hungover/beta-blockers-and-alcohol) | Added blood-pressure drop, dizziness | Low to moderate |
| Cholesterol drugs | [Statins](/never-hungover/statins-and-alcohol), [atorvastatin](/never-hungover/atorvastatin-and-alcohol) | Liver workload | Low at moderate drinking |
| Erectile dysfunction drugs | [Viagra](/never-hungover/viagra-and-alcohol) | Added blood-pressure drop | Low to moderate |
| Sedating antihistamines | Diphenhydramine (Benadryl), [hydroxyzine](/never-hungover/hydroxyzine-and-alcohol) ([all antihistamines](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol)) | Stacked sedation | Moderate to high |
| Non-drowsy antihistamines | [Zyrtec](/never-hungover/zyrtec-and-alcohol), Claritin, Allegra | Mild added drowsiness | Low |

If your medicine isn't on this list, that doesn't mean it's safe with alcohol. It means you should check its label or ask a pharmacist.

## Our Medication Class Guides

Each guide below covers one family of medicines in more depth. The one-line summaries are general patterns, not rules for your situation. Your pharmacist can tell you in a couple of minutes how your specific drug, dose, and other medicines change the picture, so treat these pages as a way to prepare good questions.

- **[Sleep aids](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol):** prescription sleeping pills, sedating antihistamines, and herbal sedatives all stack with alcohol's sedation. Don't combine them on nights you drink.
- **[Anxiety medication](/never-hungover/anxiety-medication-and-alcohol):** benzodiazepines plus alcohol can slow breathing dangerously. Other anxiety medicines carry less risk but still add drowsiness.
- **[Muscle relaxers](/never-hungover/muscle-relaxers-and-alcohol):** strong added sedation and dizziness. Avoid alcohol while taking them.
- **[Antidepressants](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol):** mostly added drowsiness and worse mood, with bigger concerns for bupropion and MAOIs. Ask before drinking.
- **[ADHD medication](/never-hungover/adhd-medication-and-alcohol):** stimulants can hide how drunk you are and add strain on the heart, so it's easy to drink more than you realize.
- **[Antihistamines](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol):** older, sedating ones stack with alcohol. Newer non-drowsy ones usually add only mild drowsiness.
- **[Antibiotics](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol):** most have no direct interaction, but a few (metronidazole and tinidazole especially) cause a severe reaction.
- **[UTI antibiotics](/never-hungover/uti-antibiotics-and-alcohol):** usually no dangerous interaction, but alcohol irritates the bladder and can slow how fast you feel better.
- **[NSAID painkillers](/never-hungover/nsaids-and-alcohol):** ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin raise stomach-bleeding risk with alcohol. Keep doses low and take them with food.
- **[Blood thinners](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol):** alcohol adds to bleeding risk and can make warfarin levels swing. Ask your prescriber what's reasonable.
- **[Beta blockers](/never-hungover/beta-blockers-and-alcohol):** both lower blood pressure, so dizziness and fainting on standing are the main risks.
- **[Statins](/never-hungover/statins-and-alcohol):** little direct interaction at moderate drinking, but heavy drinking adds to liver strain.
- **[Steroids](/never-hungover/steroids-and-alcohol):** alcohol adds to stomach irritation, blood-sugar swings, and mood effects.
- **GLP-1 medicines** ([Wegovy](/never-hungover/wegovy-and-alcohol), which is the same drug as Ozempic; [Zepbound](/never-hungover/zepbound-and-alcohol); [Mounjaro](/never-hungover/mounjaro-and-alcohol)): no direct chemical clash, but alcohol can worsen nausea and low blood sugar, and many people find they tolerate less than before.

## Which Medications Should Never Be Mixed With Alcohol?

A short list deserves a firm "don't," because the downside is a hospital visit or worse, not a bad morning.

- **Opioid painkillers.** Oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, codeine, tramadol, and others. Combined with alcohol, they can slow breathing to a dangerous degree, and some extended-release versions can release too much medicine at once.
- **Benzodiazepines.** Alprazolam (Xanax), clonazepam (Klonopin), diazepam (Valium), lorazepam (Ativan). Alcohol and benzodiazepines act on overlapping brain systems, and this combination shows up again and again in overdose reports.
- **Prescription sleeping pills.** Zolpidem (Ambien) and similar drugs carry an FDA boxed warning about "complex sleep behaviors," such as sleepwalking and sleep-driving with no memory of it. Alcohol makes these episodes more likely.
- **Metronidazole and tinidazole.** Possible severe flushing, vomiting, and racing heart. Wait 3 days after the last dose.
- **MAO inhibitors.** An older class of antidepressants. Tap beer, some wines, and other fermented drinks can contain tyramine, which can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure in people on MAOIs.

If you take any of these and you're planning to be somewhere with drinking, the safest plan is not to drink. If that's not realistic for you, talk honestly with your prescriber. They've heard it before, and they can sometimes adjust timing or switch drugs.

## Can You Drink on Medication? It Depends on Three Things

For everything outside that "never" list, the answer is usually "it depends." Three factors carry most of the weight.

**What the drug does.** A sedating medicine is a different conversation from a cholesterol pill. If your medicine's label says it may cause drowsiness, assume alcohol will make that worse.

**How much you drink.** Most label warnings and studies focus on heavy or regular drinking. The acetaminophen and NSAID labels both use "3 or more drinks every day" as their threshold. One glass of wine with dinner is a very different exposure from a night of six drinks, even with the same pill.

**Who you are.** The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), in its "Harmful Interactions" guide, singles out older adults as being at higher risk, because people metabolize alcohol and drugs more slowly with age and are more likely to take several medicines. Women generally reach higher blood alcohol levels than men from the same number of drinks. Liver disease, kidney disease, and taking several sedating medicines all raise the stakes too.

## How Long After Taking Medication Can You Drink?

There's no single waiting time that works for every drug, and you should be skeptical of any article that gives one. The right gap depends on how long the specific drug stays in your body, which varies from a few hours to several days or more.

A few useful rules of thumb:

- **For drugs you take every day** (antidepressants, blood pressure pills, statins, diabetes drugs), there is no "wait" because the drug is always in your system. The question is whether and how much you drink at all, which is one for your prescriber.
- **For short courses** (antibiotics, a few days of a painkiller), the label sometimes tells you directly. Metronidazole and tinidazole say 3 days after the last dose. For most other antibiotics, see our guide on [how long after antibiotics you can drink](/never-hungover/how-long-after-antibiotics-can-you-drink).
- **For as-needed drugs** (a sleeping pill, a muscle relaxant, an antihistamine), the sedating effects usually outlast the time you feel them. Don't take one to "come down" after drinking, and don't drink the evening after taking one without checking how long it lasts.
- **The other direction matters too.** Alcohol stays in your blood for hours after your last drink. As a rough guide, your body clears about one standard drink per hour, but this varies a lot. Taking a sedating pill at 1 a.m. after drinking all evening is still mixing them.

## Over-the-Counter Medicines Are Where Social Drinkers Get Caught

People tend to respect prescription warnings and ignore the ones on things they buy at the pharmacy shelf. But most of the alcohol interactions a typical social drinker will actually run into are over-the-counter.

**Painkillers.** The most common one. Taking ibuprofen or Tylenol for a hangover is extremely common, and both have alcohol warnings for different reasons. If you're deciding between them, our comparison of [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) walks through the trade-off. Short version: acetaminophen is harder on the liver, NSAIDs are harder on the stomach and kidneys, and neither should be taken "pre-emptively" before bed.

**Night-time cold and flu products.** These often combine acetaminophen with a sedating antihistamine, and some liquid versions contain alcohol themselves. That's two separate interactions in one bottle. If you need a cold medicine while drinking is on the table, see our guide to [alcohol-free cold medicine](/never-hungover/alcohol-free-cold-medicine) and check whether your product [contains alcohol](/never-hungover/does-cough-syrup-have-alcohol).

**Sleep aids.** Most OTC sleep aids are diphenhydramine or doxylamine, the same sedating antihistamines found in Benadryl and NyQuil. Taking one after drinking to get to sleep is a common habit and a bad one. Alcohol already wrecks the second half of your night's sleep; adding a sedative on top mostly adds next-day grogginess and, at higher doses, real risk. If drinking is keeping you up, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) has better options.

**Decongestants.** Pseudoephedrine ([Sudafed](/never-hungover/sudafed-and-alcohol)) is a stimulant. It doesn't stack sedation, but it can add to a racing heart and make it harder to notice how drunk you are.

**Antacids.** Tums, Pepcid, and omeprazole have little direct interaction with alcohol. The catch is that alcohol is often what's causing the heartburn, so the medicine is fighting the drink.

## Antibiotics and Alcohol: The Biggest Myth in This Space

Many people believe all antibiotics are dangerous with alcohol, or that drinking makes antibiotics stop working. Neither is generally true.

For most common antibiotics, including amoxicillin, azithromycin, and cephalexin, there's no major direct interaction at moderate drinking levels. Our guide on [whether alcohol makes antibiotics less effective](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-make-antibiotics-less-effective) explains what the research shows. That said, alcohol can dehydrate you, disturb your sleep, and add to stomach upset, none of which helps you get over an infection. Doctors often suggest skipping alcohol until you're better simply because your body has other work to do.

The exceptions are the ones covered above (metronidazole and tinidazole) plus a few antibiotics with their own specific concerns. For example, [doxycycline](/never-hungover/doxycycline-and-alcohol) levels can fall in chronic heavy drinkers, and [ciprofloxacin](/never-hungover/ciprofloxacin-and-alcohol) and [Bactrim](/never-hungover/bactrim-and-alcohol) have their own notes. Our [antibiotics and alcohol overview](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) covers the full class.

## Antidepressants, Anxiety Medicines, and Alcohol

This is one of the most searched groups, and one where "it depends" is genuinely the answer.

**SSRIs and SNRIs** (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, duloxetine, and others) don't usually cause a dangerous chemical reaction with a drink or two. Their labels still advise avoiding alcohol, for good reasons. Alcohol can add to drowsiness and impaired coordination, it's a depressant that can worsen the very mood or anxiety symptoms the drug is treating, and many people find they feel drunker than usual. Duloxetine (Cymbalta) has an extra liver caution for people who drink heavily.

**Bupropion (Wellbutrin)** is different. It lowers the seizure threshold, and both heavy drinking and suddenly stopping heavy drinking can raise seizure risk.

**Buspirone** is generally less sedating than benzodiazepines, but its label still advises against alcohol. See our [buspirone and alcohol](/never-hungover/buspirone-and-alcohol) guide.

**Benzodiazepines** belong on the "never" list above.

The practical advice: if you're on one of these and want to drink occasionally, raise it with your prescriber at your next appointment. Don't skip doses on drinking nights, because missing doses of some antidepressants can cause withdrawal-type symptoms of its own.

## Heart, Blood Pressure, and Diabetes Medicines

These are mostly daily medicines, so the question is less about timing and more about patterns.

**Blood pressure drugs.** Alcohol widens blood vessels and can lower blood pressure in the hours after drinking. Add a blood pressure medicine and you may feel dizzy or lightheaded, especially when standing up quickly. Over the longer term, regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure, working against the medicine. Our guide on [alcohol and blood pressure management](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) goes deeper.

**Blood thinners.** Both alcohol and blood thinners can raise bleeding risk, and alcohol makes falls more likely. Warfarin users have the added problem that drinking changes their INR (the blood test that measures clotting). Newer drugs like apixaban (Eliquis) are less sensitive to diet, but the bleeding concern still applies.

**Diabetes drugs.** The biggest risk is low blood sugar, which can look a lot like being drunk (confusion, slurred speech, unsteadiness), so people around you may not realize what's happening. It can also show up hours later, overnight. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, eat when you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and make sure someone you're with knows you have diabetes. Metformin's label also warns that excessive alcohol raises the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis. See [alcohol and blood sugar management](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) for more.

## Alcohol, Medications, and Hangovers

There's one more interaction people rarely think about: medication can make the morning after worse. Sedating drugs add to next-day grogginess. Drugs that cause dehydration or stomach upset add to the nausea and headache. And some people treat a hangover by stacking several products (a painkiller, a cold medicine "for the headache," a sleep aid the next night) without noticing they've taken acetaminophen three times.

A few practical habits help:

- **Read the active ingredients, not the brand name.** Look for acetaminophen (often listed as APAP), diphenhydramine, doxylamine, and dextromethorphan.
- **Use one product at a time** and keep a quick count of what you've taken in the past 24 hours.
- **Eat and drink water** before reaching for a pill. Many hangover symptoms ease with food, fluids, and sleep alone.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most mild interactions just mean you feel unusually drunk or unwell. But some symptoms point to something more serious, and you shouldn't wait them out.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if someone who mixed alcohol with a medicine:**

- Can't be woken, or is very hard to wake
- Is breathing slowly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute), irregularly, or making snoring or gurgling sounds
- Has blue, gray, or very pale lips or fingertips
- Has a seizure
- Has chest pain, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, or fainting
- Is vomiting while very drowsy (choking risk)

While you wait, keep them on their side, don't leave them alone, and don't give them anything else to "sober them up." If an opioid may be involved and naloxone (Narcan) is available, give it, because it's safe to use even if you're not sure. Naloxone won't reverse alcohol or benzodiazepines, so still call for help.

**Call your doctor or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if:**

- You took more than the labeled dose of a medicine and drank
- You feel severely flushed, sick, and shaky after drinking on a new medicine
- You notice unusual bruising, bleeding, black stools, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds while on a blood thinner or NSAID
- You have yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs

## A Better Path: Make the Night Itself Easier on Your Body

Most of what this guide covers boils down to one principle: the less alcohol in your system, the less there is to interact with. If you take a daily medicine and still want to drink socially, the habits that help are simple. Drink less and drink slower, eat before and during, alternate with water, and keep your medicine routine steady rather than skipping doses. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also look at supplements. Here's an honest view of DHM (dihydromyricetin), the plant compound this site focuses on. Most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies on alcohol metabolism and the liver, with a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven. It does **not** make it safe to mix alcohol with any medication on the "never" list, and there's no good evidence that it reduces the risk of any interaction described here. DHM may also interact with some medicines itself, so check our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and ask your pharmacist before adding it if you take a prescription. If you don't take medication and want to try it, a simple, low-cost option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take. For liver-focused options, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

## The Bottom Line

- Most alcohol-medication interactions come from four mechanisms: stacked sedation, shared organ stress, changes in how the liver clears a drug, and blocked alcohol breakdown.
- Opioids, benzodiazepines, prescription sleeping pills, metronidazole and tinidazole, and MAOIs should not be mixed with alcohol.
- For everything else, the answer depends on the drug, how much you drink, and your own health. One drink is a different question from a night out.
- Over-the-counter painkillers, cold medicines, and sleep aids are where social drinkers most often get caught. Read the active ingredients.
- A pharmacist can check your specific medicine against alcohol in a few minutes. Ask before you mix, not after.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What medications should you not mix with alcohol?**

The firmest "don't mix" list is opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines (such as Xanax, Klonopin, and Valium), prescription sleeping pills (such as Ambien), the antibiotics metronidazole and tinidazole, and MAO inhibitor antidepressants. Many other drugs, including sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, gabapentin, and some antidepressants, carry strong label warnings too. Check your medicine's label or ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Can you drink alcohol while on medication?**

It depends on the medicine, how much you drink, and your health. Some drugs, like most statins and many antibiotics, have little direct interaction with moderate drinking. Others, especially anything that causes drowsiness, can become dangerous with alcohol. Your medicine's label and your pharmacist are the best sources for your specific drug and dose.

**How long after taking medicine can I drink alcohol?**

There's no single waiting time for all drugs, because they stay in the body for very different lengths of time. Metronidazole and tinidazole labels say to wait 3 days after the last dose. For daily medicines, the drug is always in your system, so the question is whether to drink at all. For as-needed drugs, ask a pharmacist how long that specific medicine lasts.

**Why is mixing alcohol and medication dangerous?**

Alcohol can add to a drug's effects (for example, stacking sedation until breathing slows), stress the same organ (such as the liver or stomach), change how fast the liver clears a drug, or, with a few drugs, block alcohol breakdown and cause a toxic reaction. Which of these applies depends on the medicine.

**Is one drink okay on medication?**

For many daily medicines, one drink is unlikely to cause a serious problem, and many label warnings focus on heavy or regular drinking. But for opioids, benzodiazepines, sleeping pills, metronidazole, and MAOIs, even small amounts are a real risk. Ask your doctor or pharmacist what's reasonable for your specific medicine.

**Do antibiotics stop working if you drink alcohol?**

For most common antibiotics, moderate drinking doesn't stop them working. The main exceptions are metronidazole and tinidazole, which can cause a severe reaction with alcohol, and a few others with specific concerns. Alcohol can still slow your recovery by disturbing sleep and hydration, so many doctors suggest skipping it until you feel better.

**Can you take ibuprofen or Tylenol after drinking?**

A single normal dose the morning after a few drinks is unlikely to harm a healthy adult, but each has its own risk. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is harder on the liver, while ibuprofen and other NSAIDs are harder on the stomach and kidneys. Don't take either before bed "just in case," and if you have 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor before using them.

**Who is most at risk from alcohol-medication interactions?**

Older adults, people taking several medicines, people with liver or kidney disease, and people who drink heavily or regularly are at higher risk. Anyone taking a sedating medicine is also in a higher-risk group, because those combinations can affect breathing.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on medication?**

No. There's no good evidence that DHM reduces the risk of any alcohol-medication interaction, and DHM itself may interact with some medicines. If you take a prescription, ask your pharmacist before adding any supplement.
